specPoints.text: practical: investigate the specific heat capacity of materials including water and some solids

primer.text: Here the ΔQ = mcΔT equation is turned around and measured, not just used. An immersion heater delivers counted joules into a known mass, a thermometer logs the rise, and the gradient machinery of the plotted graph yields the capacity of water or a solid block — with honest error analysis attached.

lessons.title: Aim and variables of the SHC investigation
lessons.opening: The aim is to measure a specific heat capacity from first principles: supply counted electrical energy to a known mass and watch the temperature respond. Naming the variables precisely is what turns a heating demonstration into a fair test.
keyPoints: The aim is to determine the specific heat capacity of water or a solid material.
The independent variable is the energy supplied by the heater.
The dependent variable is the temperature rise of the material.
The mass of material and the starting temperature are controlled variables.
Energy supplied is computed from the heater's voltage, current and heating time.

low.restatement: Heat a known mass with an electric heater, count the energy from voltage times current times time, and measure how many degrees the mass climbs. Divide the energy by the mass and the rise to get the capacity.
low.analogy: Metering a taxi journey: the meter (heater) counts the fare (energy), the passengers (mass) and distance (degrees) are known, so the per-passenger-per-kilometre rate (capacity) can be worked out.
low.examPointer: Variable-naming marks are free if you keep the roles straight: energy supplied is what you change, temperature rise is what you measure, mass is what you hold fixed.

medium.restatement: The design computes ΔQ as VIt from ammeter and voltmeter readings timed with a stopwatch, so the energy is known without calorimetry assumptions. Controlling the mass pins the proportionality between energy and temperature rise, and the starting temperature is held near room value to limit unquantified exchange with the surroundings.
medium.analogy: Calibrating a fuel gauge by driving a known distance at a metered flow: fix the tank size (mass), count the litres (energy), read the needle (temperature), and the car's thirst per kilometre emerges.
medium.examPointer: If asked why the heater is switched off between readings or readings taken while switching on and off, answer energy accounting — every second of heating counts, including brief overshoots.

check.stem: What is the aim of this investigation into specific heat capacity?

options.text: to find the specific heat capacity of water or another material
options.explanation: The measurement of c from supplied energy and temperature rise is the target.

options.text: to observe a constant temperature during melting
options.explanation: That is the changes-of-state practical.

options.text: to measure the latent heat of vaporisation
options.explanation: No boiling occurs in this investigation.

options.text: to compare the densities of liquids
options.explanation: Density is a different topic entirely.

check.stem: Which is the independent variable in this investigation?

options.text: the energy supplied by the heater
options.explanation: Energy in is what the experimenter controls and changes.

options.text: the temperature rise of the material
options.explanation: The rise is measured, making it the dependent variable.

options.text: the mass of the material
options.explanation: Mass is held fixed — a control variable.

options.text: the room temperature
options.explanation: Room conditions are background controls, not the manipulated input.

check.stem: How is the energy supplied by the immersion heater calculated?

options.text: voltage × current × heating time
options.explanation: E = VIt is the electrical energy delivered.

options.text: voltage × current
options.explanation: That is power; the heating time factor is missing.

options.text: mass × temperature rise
options.explanation: That product has no energy meaning without the capacity.

options.text: current ÷ time
options.explanation: Charge per second is not energy.

check.stem: Why is the mass of the liquid a control variable?

options.text: the temperature rise per joule depends on the mass, so it must be fixed for a fair test
options.explanation: ΔQ = mcΔT ties the response to the mass.

options.text: changing the mass would break the thermometer
options.explanation: The risk is unfair comparison, not equipment damage.

options.text: mass cannot be measured in a laboratory
options.explanation: A balance measures it easily.

options.text: mass is the dependent variable
options.explanation: Temperature rise is the dependent variable.

check.stem: A student starts with water at 5 °C on a cold bench instead of near room temperature. Why does this threaten the accuracy?

options.text: the large temperature gap with the surroundings adds uncontrolled energy exchange
options.explanation: Cold water draws in heat from the room, corrupting the energy account.

options.text: the thermometer cannot read 5 °C
options.explanation: Ordinary lab thermometers read far below 5 °C.

options.text: the heater stops working below 10 °C
options.explanation: Immersion heaters work at any starting temperature.

options.text: water has no specific heat capacity at 5 °C
options.explanation: The capacity is defined at all temperatures within the liquid state.

check.stem: State the independent and dependent variables of this practical.
check.modelAnswer: The independent variable is the energy supplied by the heater; the dependent variable is the resulting temperature rise of the material.

check.stem: State the equation used to compute the electrical energy supplied to the heater.
check.modelAnswer: Energy = voltage × current × time, E = V × I × t.

check.stem: Explain why the starting temperature is controlled near room temperature in this investigation.
check.modelAnswer: The energy account assumes all the heater's joules go into the sample. If the sample starts well below room temperature, the surroundings donate extra heat during the run; if well above, the sample leaks heat out. Starting near room temperature keeps that unmeasured exchange small, so c = ΔQ ÷ (mΔT) stays honest.

check.stem: A heater runs at 10 V and 2.0 A for 500 s. Calculate the energy supplied.

lessons.title: Equipment, method and the heating set-up
sourceHeadings: The experiment set up for the specific heat capacity practical
lessons.opening: The set-up is an insulated beaker, a known mass of water, an immersion heater wired to meters, and a thermometer watching the rise. The method is an energy ledger: read the meters, time the run, log the temperature on the beat.
keyPoints: The kit comprises a balance, insulated beaker, immersion heater, voltmeter, ammeter, stopwatch and thermometer.
The mass of water is measured on the balance before heating begins.
The heater is switched on and the meters read at the same time as the stopwatch starts.
Temperature readings are taken at regular intervals while the heater runs.
The set-up keeps the heater fully submerged so all delivered energy enters the water.

low.restatement: Weigh the water, drop in the heater, wire up the meters, and switch on while starting the clock. Note the temperature every half-minute and read the meters so the energy can be counted.
low.analogy: A cooking show with a scoreboard: the balance weighs the pot, the meters count the gas, the thermometer reports the result every round.
low.examPointer: Method marks live in the sequence: mass first, then meters zeroed and read, then heating with timed temperature readings — describe the order, not just the list.

medium.restatement: The apparatus couples electrical metering to thermal sensing so that ΔQ is known independently of the water's properties. Full submersion and lagging minimise the two leakage classes — energy bypassing the water and heat escaping to air — while fixed-interval sampling turns the run into an energy-versus-temperature dataset suitable for a gradient method.
medium.analogy: An audit trail: every joule is receipted by the meters (VIt), every degree is receipted by the thermometer, and the auditor (the calculation) compares the two books.
medium.examPointer: Quote the insulation purpose explicitly — lagging reduces the systematic error of heat lost to the surroundings, which otherwise inflates the measured capacity.

check.stem: Which instrument measures the mass of the water before heating?

options.text: a balance
options.explanation: The known mass comes from the balance reading.

options.text: a measuring cylinder
options.explanation: A cylinder measures volume; converting to mass invites density error.

options.text: the ammeter
options.explanation: The ammeter reads current.

options.text: the thermometer
options.explanation: The thermometer reads temperature.

check.stem: Why must the immersion heater be fully submerged?

options.text: so all the electrical energy is delivered into the water
options.explanation: Exposed heater sections waste energy to air, corrupting ΔQ.

options.text: so the water cannot boil
options.explanation: Submersion has nothing to do with suppressing boiling.

options.text: so the meters read more accurately
options.explanation: Meter accuracy is independent of submersion.

options.text: so the thermometer fits alongside
options.explanation: Thermometer placement is a separate matter.

check.stem: When should the stopwatch be started?

options.text: at the same moment the heater is switched on
options.explanation: The energy ledger and the clock must open together.

options.text: five minutes after heating starts
options.explanation: A late start loses energy from the account.

options.text: after the first temperature reading
options.explanation: The first reading belongs to the timed sequence.

options.text: when the water starts warming
options.explanation: Warming begins almost immediately; the switch-on moment is the reference.

check.stem: Why is the beaker lagged or insulated in this set-up?

options.text: to reduce energy lost to the surroundings, a systematic error
options.explanation: Insulation keeps the measured ΔQ closer to the energy the water actually received.

options.text: to stop the water from changing state
options.explanation: The water is not meant to change state anyway at these temperatures.

options.text: to make the heater more powerful
options.explanation: Insulation does not change the heater's power.

options.text: to hold the thermometer upright
options.explanation: A stand does that job.

check.stem: A student reads the voltmeter only at the end of the run. Why is this poor practice?

options.text: the supply can drift during the run, so the energy account needs readings throughout
options.explanation: E = VIt assumes steady V and I; only monitoring proves it.

options.text: voltmeters drain their batteries if read twice
options.explanation: Reading a voltmeter does not drain anything.

options.text: the final voltage is always wrong
options.explanation: A single reading is not always wrong; it is just unverified.

options.text: the voltmeter must be read by two students
options.explanation: Crew size is irrelevant to drift.

check.stem: State the full equipment list for measuring the specific heat capacity of water.
check.modelAnswer: A balance, insulated beaker, immersion heater, voltmeter, ammeter, stopwatch and thermometer.

check.stem: State what should be measured before the heater is switched on.
check.modelAnswer: The mass of the water on the balance, plus the initial temperature of the water and the meter readings.

check.stem: Explain why the voltmeter and ammeter are read during the run and not only at the end.
check.modelAnswer: The energy ledger uses E = VIt, which multiplies an average voltage and current by the time. If the supply sags or surges partway through, end-point readings misrepresent the energy actually delivered. Periodic meter readings verify that V and I stayed steady, or allow an averaged product to be used, keeping ΔQ honest.

check.stem: A run delivers 10 000 J to 1.0 kg of water and the temperature climbs from 14 °C to 30 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity this suggests.
check.modelAnswer: ΔT = 30 − 14 = 16 °C, so c = ΔQ ÷ (m × ΔT) = 10 000 ÷ (1.0 × 16) = 625 J/kg °C — far below water's 4200, pointing to energy lost or misdelivered in the set-up.

lessons.title: Results table and the energy ledger
sourceHeadings: An example of a results table for the specific heat capacity practical
lessons.opening: The results live in two books: the meters' energy ledger and the thermometer's temperature column. Tabulating both against time lets every joule be matched to every degree at the moment it arrived.
keyPoints: The table records time, temperature, and the meter readings at each interval.
Energy supplied is accumulated as voltage × current × elapsed time.
Each temperature is paired with the energy delivered up to that moment.
The energy-per-degree relationship becomes visible once the table is complete.

low.restatement: Every half-minute, write down the clock, the temperature, and the meters. Multiply voltage by current by the seconds elapsed to stack up the energy next to each temperature.
low.analogy: A shared spreadsheet: one column counts money in (energy), another counts the rise it bought (temperature), and each row is a receipt.
low.examPointer: The table earns marks when the energy column is cumulative and aligned with each temperature — a mismatched ledger loses the analysis marks later.

medium.restatement: Structuring the table with a cumulative energy column converts the run into paired (ΔQ, ΔT) points suitable for plotting energy against temperature rise. Because ΔQ = mcΔT, the gradient of that plot equals m × c, so the ledger format feeds directly into the gradient analysis rather than relying on a single end-point ratio.
medium.analogy: Mileage versus fuel burned, logged at every petrol stop: the slope of the log reveals the car's consumption far better than one end-to-end division.
medium.examPointer: If the table shows the temperature levelling while energy keeps flowing, suspect a state change or a heater fault — do not force the linear analysis through curved data.

check.stem: Which columns belong in the results table?

options.text: time, temperature, and meter readings for voltage and current
options.explanation: Together they let energy be computed against each temperature.

options.text: colour and smell of the water
options.explanation: Qualitative observations are not part of this quantitative ledger.

options.text: only the final temperature
options.explanation: A single reading cannot support the analysis.

options.text: the student's names per interval
options.explanation: Roles may be noted elsewhere, not in the data table.

check.stem: How is the cumulative energy at each interval obtained?

options.text: voltage × current × the elapsed heating time
options.explanation: E = VIt with the running clock gives the accumulated energy.

options.text: adding all the temperature readings so far
options.explanation: Temperatures are not additive into energy.

options.text: multiplying the mass by the elapsed time
options.explanation: Mass times time has no energy meaning.

options.text: reading it from the thermometer
options.explanation: The thermometer reads temperature, not energy.

check.stem: Why pair each temperature with the energy delivered up to that moment?

options.text: the paired points let energy be plotted against temperature rise for a gradient method
options.explanation: Paired data is what the ΔQ–ΔT plot needs.

options.text: pairing makes the table look fuller
options.explanation: Presentation is not the purpose.

options.text: pairing is required by the exam board's form
options.explanation: The pairing serves the physics, not paperwork.

options.text: unpaired readings are invalid units
options.explanation: The readings are valid; pairing is for the analysis.

check.stem: In the results-table image for this practical, what does the caption note about energy supplied?

options.text: energy supplied equals voltage × current × time
options.explanation: The caption restates the E = VIt ledger law.

options.text: energy supplied equals mass × temperature rise
options.explanation: That is missing the capacity and the wrong ledger entirely.

options.text: energy supplied is read from the thermometer
options.explanation: Thermometers never read energy.

options.text: energy supplied is constant whatever the meters say
options.explanation: The meters define the energy.

check.stem: A table shows energy climbing in equal steps while the temperature rise per step shrinks. What does that suggest?

options.text: energy is leaking from the system faster as the water gets hotter
options.explanation: Hotter water loses more to the surroundings, so less of each step warms it.

options.text: the water's specific heat capacity is falling during the run
options.explanation: The capacity is effectively constant; leakage explains the curve.

options.text: the thermometer is broken
options.explanation: A systematic flattening points to leakage, not breakage.

options.text: the meters are adding wrongly
options.explanation: Equal energy steps are exactly what steady meters show.

check.stem: State what each row of the results table represents.
check.modelAnswer: Each row is one timed interval: the clock time, the temperature read then, and the meter readings that fix the energy delivered by then.

check.stem: State the relationship the completed table is designed to reveal.
check.modelAnswer: It shows the proportionality between the energy supplied and the temperature rise, whose ratio through the mass gives the specific heat capacity.

check.stem: Explain why a cumulative energy column is more useful than recording energy only at the end of the run.
check.modelAnswer: A cumulative column turns the run into many paired (energy, temperature) points, so the analysis can use the gradient of the whole dataset instead of trusting one end-point division. It also exposes any non-linearity — drift, leakage, boiling — that a single final figure would silently hide.

check.stem: A heater delivers 10 000 J in total and the table's final temperature rise is 16 °C for a 1.0 kg sample. Using c = ΔQ ÷ (mΔT), calculate the capacity the table suggests and compare it to water's 4200 J/kg °C.
check.modelAnswer: c = 10 000 ÷ (1.0 × 16) = 625 J/kg °C. That is far below 4200 J/kg °C, so only a fraction of the heater's energy actually warmed the sample — losses dominated the ledger.

lessons.title: Analysis by gradient, evaluation and safety
sourceHeadings: Analysis of specific heat capacity practical results
An example graph for the specific heat capacity practical
lessons.opening: Plot the ledger and the slope speaks: gradient one over mass times capacity gives the answer, provided the joules all landed — which is where losses, repetition and mains safety take over the evaluation.
keyPoints: Plot temperature rise on the vertical axis against energy supplied on the horizontal axis.
The gradient of the line equals 1 ÷ (m × c), so c = 1 ÷ (m × gradient).
Heat lost to the surroundings is the main systematic error and makes the measured c too high.
Lagging the beaker and fully submerging the heater cut the dominant systematic loss.
Parallax and reaction-time wobble are random errors, reduced by repetition and smoothing.
Mains heaters demand dry hands, insulated leads, eye protection and safe handling of scalding water.

low.restatement: Take the slope, divide one by mass times slope, and the capacity appears — as long as no joules leaked, so lag the beaker, repeat the run, and keep the mains wiring dry and guarded.
low.analogy: A scales-and-tilt audit: read the honest line (gradient), fence off the leak (lagging), take several weighings (repetition), and keep the plug socket dry throughout.
low.examPointer: Order the evaluation: name the error, give its direction on c, then the fix — and keep every mains-safety point separate from the thermal analysis.

medium.restatement: Rearranging ΔQ = mcΔT gives ΔT = (1/mc)·ΔQ, so the fitted slope yields c for the fixed mass; the dominant systematic term is unaccounted power dissipated outside the sample, biasing c upward, while parallax and timing scatter are random and average out over repeats. Mains safety — dry hands, insulated leads, supervised switching — is a separate, non-negotiable layer.
medium.analogy: Auditing a delivery route: the odometer counts every kilometre including detours, so the true fuel-per-kilometre needs the detours fenced (lagging) and several runs averaged (repetition) — all with the driver gloved and grounded.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish the two bias directions before naming fixes: losses and an underestimated rise both inflate c, while a mass overestimate would deflate it — then separate the mains-safety list from the thermal list.

check.stem: What is plotted on each axis for the gradient analysis?

options.text: temperature rise vertically, energy supplied horizontally
options.explanation: That orientation gives gradient = ΔT/ΔQ = 1/(mc).

options.text: energy vertically, temperature rise horizontally
options.explanation: That inversion makes the gradient mc instead — workable but not the of-record layout.

options.text: time on both axes
options.explanation: Time is the sampling rhythm, not an analysis axis here.

options.text: mass vertically, voltage horizontally
options.explanation: Mass is fixed; voltage is an intermediate reading.

check.stem: What does the gradient of the ΔT–ΔQ line equal?

options.explanation: From ΔT = (1/mc)·ΔQ with mass fixed.

options.text: m × c
options.explanation: That is the reciprocal layout's gradient.

options.text: c on its own
options.explanation: The mass factor must be divided out.

options.text: ΔQ × ΔT
options.explanation: Gradients are ratios of changes, not products.

check.stem: How does heat lost to the surroundings bias the measured specific heat capacity?

options.text: it makes the measured value too high, because ΔQ is overcounted for the rise achieved
options.explanation: c = ΔQ/(mΔT) grows when ΔQ includes joules that never warmed the sample.

options.text: it makes the measured value too low
options.explanation: Missing energy from the sample's side, not excess, would lower it.

options.text: it has no effect because the meters are accurate
options.explanation: The meters are accurate about energy delivered — including the wasted part.

options.text: it makes the value random rather than biased
options.explanation: Leakage is repeatable and one-directional — systematic.

check.stem: Which improvement most directly reduces the dominant systematic error?

options.text: lagging the beaker and keeping the heater fully submerged
options.explanation: Both cut the energy that leaves the sample unaccounted.

options.text: reading the thermometer from directly above
options.explanation: That reduces parallax, a random error, not leakage.

options.text: using a shorter stopwatch
options.explanation: Timing precision is not the systematic driver.

options.text: writing neater tables
options.explanation: Presentation does not change the physics.

check.stem: Which pair lists one random and one systematic error of this practical?

options.text: parallax on the thermometer (random) and heat loss through the beaker (systematic)
options.explanation: Scatter versus repeatable bias — correctly classified.

options.text: heat loss (random) and parallax (systematic)
options.explanation: Both are swapped.

options.text: parallax and parallax
options.explanation: One error cannot be both classes.

options.text: neither error exists in this practical
options.explanation: Both classes are present in any heating run.

check.stem: State the relation between the graph's gradient and the specific heat capacity.
check.modelAnswer: Gradient = ΔT ÷ ΔQ = 1 ÷ (m × c), so the specific heat capacity equals 1 divided by the product of mass and gradient.

check.stem: State two safety precautions specific to using an electric immersion heater with water.
check.modelAnswer: Keep hands dry and use insulated leads when connecting the mains-powered heater, and protect against scalding hot water with eye protection and safe handling.

check.stem: Explain why the first few points of the graph often sit closest to the ideal straight line, and why repeating the run with a fresh cool sample tightens the result.
check.modelAnswer: Early in the run the sample is near room temperature, so the surroundings gap — and therefore the leaked power — is smallest and almost all the metered energy warms the water. Repetition with a fresh cool sample keeps that gap small again and averages the random scatter of thermometer and stopwatch readings, pulling the fitted gradient towards the ideal proportional line.

check.stem: A 1.0 kg sample's ΔT–ΔQ line has a gradient of 0.0016 °C/J over its linear region. Calculate the specific heat capacity.

glossary.definition: An electric heater designed to transfer its energy directly into a liquid it is submerged in.
A repeatable bias that shifts results in one direction, such as heat loss inflating capacity.
Deriving a property from the slope of a best-fit line through many paired readings.
Insulation wrapped around a vessel to reduce energy exchange with the surroundings.
